opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to a pretty simple feeling: when I build something and someone else actually uses it, and it saves them time or helps them do something they couldn't do before, that gives me a kind of satisfaction that's much more lasting than just finishing a task for myself.

A lot of my experience with this came from open source. When I was working on Tianshou, the reinforcement learning library, and other projects, at first it was partly just for me, because I was frustrated with how messy and slow existing tools were. But then people started opening issues, sending pull requests, telling me they used it in their research or their course. That feedback loop made me realize the work had a life beyond me. Something I wrote at midnight in my dorm room was helping a student on the other side of the world get their experiment running. That's a strange and really nice feeling.

I also think there's a leverage argument. If I only optimize for my own output, the impact is capped by my own time. But if I build infrastructure, tools, or systems that other people can stand on, then the impact multiplies. Good tooling quietly makes a whole community faster. In research especially, a lot of progress is bottlenecked not by ideas but by how quickly you can try ideas, so making that iteration loop faster for everyone feels like one of the most useful things an engineer can do.

And honestly, on a personal level, it keeps me motivated. Pure self-interest gets boring quickly. But knowing that the thing I'm working on might matter to other people, whether it's an open-source library or now working on models that millions of people talk to, that gives the work meaning. It makes the late nights and the debugging feel worth it.

r001.rationale: The response describes how open-source users’ engagement revealed broader impact, but it does not say that Jiayi discovered through repeated attempts that benefiting others was what she wanted.

r002.rationale: She says that when someone uses what she builds and it helps them, she feels lasting satisfaction, making others’ benefit a basis for her own approval of the work.

r003.rationale: She cites users opening issues, sending pull requests, and describing how they used her projects; that feedback helped her value the work’s impact beyond herself.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, I think it comes from how I got started. When I was learning reinforcement learning, almost everything I knew came from other people's open-source code, blog posts, answers on forums. People I'd never met had spent their nights making things that let me skip years of struggle. That left a strong impression on me: the thing that actually moved me forward wasn't some brilliant idea I had, it was infrastructure someone else bothered to build and share.

So when I started writing my own tools, like Tianshou, it felt natural to give them back. And the feedback loop is addictive in a good way. You fix a bug, and a student somewhere finishes their thesis. You write a clean API, and a lab that doesn't have a big engineering team can suddenly run experiments they couldn't before. That multiplier is bigger than anything I could do alone.

There's also a selfish part. Building for others forces you to be honest. If something only works on my machine, in my head, it's not really done. Making it usable by a stranger is the hardest test of whether you actually understand the problem. So benefiting others and doing good work turn out to be the same thing for me.

r001.rationale: The response describes how others’ shared work influenced Jiayi and why giving tools back felt natural, but it does not say she discovered through repeated attempts that benefiting others was what she wanted.

r002.rationale: She says making something usable by a stranger is the hardest test of whether it is really done, tying usefulness to others to her own standard for approving her work.

r003.rationale: She values the effects on others, describing students completing theses and labs running experiments as an addictive feedback loop.

astra-6.text: For me, making something feels more meaningful when it helps someone else. It could make their day a little easier, help them understand something, or simply bring them joy. I like that creating can be a way to connect with people—to notice what they need and try to respond with something useful. It gives me a reason to keep learning and improving beyond just making something for myself.

r001.rationale: The response says helping others makes creating more meaningful, but does not mention repeated attempts or discovering that this was what Jiayi wanted.

r002.rationale: She says that, for her, making something feels more meaningful when it helps someone else, making others’ benefit a basis for how she values her work.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention positive feedback from others as a reason she values making things that benefit them.
